rows.subtopic: Factors Influencing Rate of a Reaction
rows.stem:
(a) Define rate constant.
(b) Identify the reaction order which has a rate constant of \(4{\cdot}5 \times 10^{-5}\) L \(\mathrm{mol^{-1}}\) \(\mathrm{s^{-1}}\).
rows.solution:
(a) The rate constant is the proportionality constant in the rate law — equivalently, it is the rate of the reaction when the molar concentration of every reacting species is taken as unity. Unlike the rate itself, it does not depend on concentration; it depends only on the temperature and on the nature of the reaction.

(b) Read the order off the UNITS. Rate always carries units of mol \(\mathrm{L^{-1}\ s^{-1}}\), so for order \(n\) the constant has units \(\mathrm{mol^{1-n}\ L^{n-1}\ s^{-1}}\). The value given, \(\mathrm{L\ mol^{-1}\ s^{-1}}\), is rate divided by concentration SQUARED, which needs \(n = 2\).
The reaction is of SECOND order.

rows.stem: Write the mechanism of dehydration of ethyl alcohol with conc. \(\mathrm{H_2SO_4}\) at 413 K.
rows.solution:
At 413 K — the LOWER of the two dehydration temperatures — ethanol gives the ETHER, not the alkene. The mechanism has three steps.

Step 1 — protonation of the alcohol. The oxygen uses a lone pair to pick up a proton from the acid, giving the protonated alcohol:
\(\mathrm{CH_3CH_2-OH} + \mathrm{H^+} \rightleftharpoons \mathrm{CH_3CH_2-\overset{+}{O}H_2}\)

Step 2 — nucleophilic attack by a SECOND alcohol molecule. The oxygen of another ethanol attacks the carbon of the protonated alcohol, displacing water in an \(\mathrm{S_N}2\) step:
\(\mathrm{CH_3CH_2-\ddot{O}H} + \mathrm{CH_3CH_2-\overset{+}{O}H_2} \longrightarrow \mathrm{CH_3CH_2-\overset{+}{O}(H)-CH_2CH_3} + \mathrm{H_2O}\)

Step 3 — deprotonation. A base removes the extra proton from the protonated ether, giving the ether and regenerating the acid:
\(\mathrm{CH_3CH_2-\overset{+}{O}(H)-CH_2CH_3} \longrightarrow \mathrm{CH_3CH_2-O-CH_2CH_3} + \mathrm{H^+}\)

The temperature is what selects the product: at 443 K the protonated alcohol loses water to a carbocation instead, and the product is ethene.

rows.subtopic: Chemical Reactions of Aldehydes and Ketones
rows.stem:
(a) Give a simple chemical test to distinguish between 3-pentanone and 2-pentanone.
(b) Write an equation for Clemmensen reduction.
rows.solution:
(a) Use the iodoform test. Warm each with sodium hydroxide and iodine: 2-pentanone has its carbonyl next to a METHYL group, so it gives a yellow precipitate of iodoform; 3-pentanone has its carbonyl between two ethyl groups and gives none.

(b) Clemmensen reduction converts a carbonyl group all the way to \(\mathrm{CH_2}\), using zinc amalgam and concentrated hydrochloric acid:
\(\mathrm{C{=}O} \xrightarrow[\mathrm{HCl}]{\mathrm{Zn\text{-}Hg}} \mathrm{CH_2} + \mathrm{H_2O}\)
It is the acidic-medium counterpart of Wolff-Kishner reduction, which achieves the same conversion in alkali.

rows.stem:
(a) Based on Valence Bond Theory, explain the geometry and magnetic character of \([\mathrm{NiCl_4}]^{2-}\). [Atomic number : Ni = 28]
(b) Draw the possible isomers of \([\mathrm{Co(en)_2Cl_2}]^{+}\).
rows.solution:
(a) Nickel is \(+2\) here, so \(\mathrm{Ni^{2+}}\) is \(3d^8\), which has two unpaired electrons. The chloride ion is a WEAK field ligand and cannot force those two to pair, so the \(3d\) set is left as it is and no inner d orbital is available for bonding. Bonding therefore uses the \(4s\) and the three \(4p\) orbitals.

Hybridisation: \(sp^3\); geometry: TETRAHEDRAL; magnetic character: PARAMAGNETIC, with two unpaired electrons — a high spin complex.

(b) \(\mathrm{[Co(en)_2Cl_2]^{+}}\) is octahedral with two bidentate ligands and two chlorides, so there are two GEOMETRICAL isomers: the CIS form, with the two chlorido ligands adjacent, and the TRANS form, with them opposite.

The trans form has a plane of symmetry and is optically inactive. The CIS form has none, so it is chiral and exists as a further pair of OPTICAL isomers — two non-superimposable mirror images. That makes three stereoisomers in all: trans, and the \(d\) and \(l\) forms of cis.

rows.stem:
(a) Among the following, which will have inversion of configuration on reaction with aqueous alkali and why ?
(i) 1-chloropropane    OR    (ii) 2-chloro-2-methylpropane
(b) Which of the following (A) or (B) will be the major product in the reaction given below ? Give a suitable reason for your answer.
\(\mathrm{CH_3-CH_2-CH(Br)-CH_3} + \text{alc. KOH} \longrightarrow\)
\(\mathrm{CH_3-CH_2-CH=CH_2}\) (A) \(+\) \(\mathrm{CH_3-CH=CH-CH_3}\) (B)
rows.solution:
(a) 1-CHLOROPROPANE will show inversion of configuration.

Inversion is the signature of the \(\mathrm{S_N}2\) route, in which the nucleophile attacks from the side opposite the leaving group and the other three bonds are pushed through to the far side in one step. That route needs an accessible carbon, and 1-chloropropane is a PRIMARY halide with a nearly unobstructed carbon. 2-Chloro-2-methylpropane is tertiary: its carbon is blocked by three methyl groups, so it reacts by \(\mathrm{S_N}1\) through a planar carbocation, which the nucleophile attacks from either face — giving racemisation, not inversion.

(b) Product (B), but-2-ene, is the major product.

Alcoholic potassium hydroxide eliminates, and by SAYTZEFF'S RULE the alkene formed in the greater amount is the one with more alkyl groups attached to the doubly bonded carbons. But-2-ene has two such groups, one on each alkene carbon; but-1-ene has only one. The more substituted alkene is the more stable, and it predominates.

rows.stem:
(a) Write the chemical equation for Williamson's synthesis.
(b) Give a method to separate \(o\)-nitrophenol and \(p\)-nitrophenol. Explain the principle involved.
rows.solution:
(a) Williamson's synthesis prepares an ether by treating an alkyl halide with a sodium alkoxide, the alkoxide displacing the halide in an \(\mathrm{S_N}2\) step:
\(\mathrm{R-X} + \mathrm{R'-ONa} \xrightarrow{\text{dry ether}} \mathrm{R-O-R'} + \mathrm{NaX}\)
Because the step is \(\mathrm{S_N}2\), the HALIDE must be primary; a tertiary halide would eliminate instead.

(b) Separate them by STEAM DISTILLATION.

The principle is a difference in HYDROGEN BONDING. In o-nitrophenol the nitro group is close enough to the hydroxyl group for the two to hydrogen bond WITHIN the same molecule — intramolecular hydrogen bonding, sometimes called chelation. That uses up the hydroxyl's bonding capacity, so the molecules do not associate with one another and the compound is volatile; it distils over with the steam.

In p-nitrophenol the two groups are too far apart for that, so the hydrogen bonding is INTERMOLECULAR: the molecules associate with one another into larger aggregates, the compound is far less volatile, and it stays behind in the flask.

rows.stem:
Identify P, Q and R in the following reaction sequence :
\(\mathrm{P} \xrightarrow{\mathrm{NH_3}} \mathrm{CH_3COO^-NH_4^+} \xrightarrow{\Delta} \mathrm{Q}\)
\(\mathrm{P} \xrightarrow{\mathrm{PCl_5}} \mathrm{R}\)
rows.figureNote: ILLUSTRATIVE - read on my own page. The sequence is printed as a two-dimensional BRANCHED scheme rather than as two separate lines: P sits at the left, one right-pointing arrow labelled \(\mathrm{NH_3}\) above it leads to \(\mathrm{CH_3COO^-NH_4^+}\) and on to Q under an arrow labelled \(\Delta\); a vertical stroke drops from P and turns right into a second arrow labelled \(\mathrm{PCl_5}\) leading to R. The stem above renders that branch losslessly by repeating P on the second line, so the row IS answerable from text. Page idx 14.
rows.solution:
The ammonium salt named in the sequence, \(\mathrm{CH_3COO^-NH_4^+}\), is ammonium acetate, so P must be the acid it comes from:
\(\mathrm{P} = \mathrm{CH_3COOH}\), ethanoic acid

Heating an ammonium carboxylate drives off water and leaves the amide:
\(\mathrm{CH_3COONH_4} \xrightarrow{\Delta} \mathrm{CH_3CONH_2} + \mathrm{H_2O}\)
\(\mathrm{Q} = \mathrm{CH_3CONH_2}\), ethanamide

Phosphorus pentachloride converts a carboxylic acid to its acyl chloride:
\(\mathrm{CH_3COOH} + \mathrm{PCl_5} \longrightarrow \mathrm{CH_3COCl} + \mathrm{POCl_3} + \mathrm{HCl}\)
\(\mathrm{R} = \mathrm{CH_3COCl}\), ethanoyl chloride

rows.stem:
(a) Name the vitamin whose deficiency causes pernicious anaemia.
(b) Write any two differences between globular and fibrous proteins.
rows.solution:
(a) Vitamin \(\mathrm{B_{12}}\), cyanocobalamin. Its deficiency causes pernicious anaemia; it is the only vitamin containing a metal atom, cobalt, at the centre of its structure.

(b) Two differences:
A GLOBULAR protein has its polypeptide chain coiled and folded back on itself into a roughly SPHERICAL shape, whereas a FIBROUS protein has its chains running parallel to one another, held side by side by hydrogen bonds and disulphide bridges, giving a THREAD-LIKE structure.
Globular proteins are generally SOLUBLE in water — insulin and albumin — whereas fibrous proteins are INSOLUBLE — keratin and myosin.

The functions follow from the shapes: globular proteins are the enzymes and hormones, fibrous ones the structural material of hair, nail and muscle.
